I work with a Clerk's office in the Metro Detroit area, although not the City of Detroit.

The State of Michigan used funds from the Help America Vote Act, which was passed after the 2000 General Election and the Florida hanging chad debacle. At that time, the State of Michigan standardized the voting machines state wide. The machines are an optical scanner, think of the old Scantron forms used for testing in school. It is similar. These machines are getting along in years. They are repairable if something happens, but the Clerk's office has to actually spend the money to fix the machines. These machines are not prone to jams, if properly maintained, but my guess is that Detroit has not properly maintained the machines. When the machine jams, it may or may not register the ballot as having been read. Sometimes it does, sometimes it doesn't. One of the problems is, at the time of scanning the ballot, if it jams, there is no immediate way to tell if the machine registered the ballot or not. What you have to wait for is at the end of the day, you close out the machine and it prints a report of the ballots counted.

Now, on the human side of the process, the election workers are supposed to record the number of ballots handed out, spoiled ballots, ballots that got destroyed by a jam in the machine, etc. Because it is mainly older folks manning the election precincts, an accurate count of the ballots used is a goal that the Clerk's office doesn't always get to achieve. I know the Clerk's office that I work with has a difficult time getting election workers as it is. I cannot imagine the mess it is in Detroit where half the population is illiterate.

At the end of the day, the count of ballots by the election workers should match the number of ballots the machine said it counted, with obvious exceptions for spoiled ballots, torn ballots, unused ballots, etc. If the numbers do not match, then the election workers have to be able to explain to the Clerks why the number doesn't match. That's the problem Detroit has. A whole bunch of machines were broken or broke down and the numbers do not match. Sometimes, you can't figure out why the numbers do not match. So the Board of Canvassers, which certify the election results, are supposed to take these discrepancies into account before certifying the election, but that doesn't mean they actually do.

Having said all that, here is where the recount stands for those precincts in Detroit. The numbers do not reconcile, we already know that. So what happens is they open the ballot containers and count the number of ballots in the container. If that matches the number of ballots the election workers said they used, then the recount can proceed. It is assumed the machine screwed up the count of ballots it scanned. However, if the number of ballots in the container doesn't match the election worker's count, then a recount cannot proceed because nobody knows which number is right. In that case, the number of votes the machine counted on the night of the election is used as the only available total. I can understand why they use that number in the event the recount is unavailable. My problem is why are you using a number from a machine that is known to be wrong just because you cannot determine what the right number is. Shouldn't that precinct just not count because it isn't accurate?
